html:
How to give people and programs exactly the access they need in each namespace, and nothing more, and what makes up a complete access-control setup (an ACL) for a cluster. Read Concepts: what each piece is first if namespaces, contexts or kubeconfig are new to you.

Not tested yet. Written from Kubernetes' documented behaviour. The hands-on parts use the kind cluster local-cluster-1 and the namespaces web, cache and db from Create a local Kubernetes cluster with kind; they work the same on k3d. Run them once and fix anything that differs on your version.

#1. The big picture: three questions, asked in order

Every request to the cluster, whether from kubectl or from a program, goes through the API server, which asks three questions in a fixed order:

QuestionNameAnswered by
Who are you?AuthenticationCertificates, tokens, or a login provider (OIDC / SSO)
Are you allowed to do this?AuthorizationRBAC (Roles and bindings): the heart of the ACL
Is this request acceptable?AdmissionRules about the object itself, such as Pod Security or quotas

A request that fails any step is refused. Most of what follows is about the middle one, RBAC.

Two facts that surprise people:

  • Kubernetes has no user accounts. There is no kubectl create user. A "user" is simply a name that your authentication method vouches for: the CN field in a certificate, or a name in an SSO token. Kubernetes only stores what that name may do.
  • RBAC only grants. There are no "deny" rules. Access is the sum of every rule that matches. No rule means no access, which is the safe default.

#2. The objects

ObjectScopeWhat it is
Roleone namespaceA list of permissions: "these verbs on these resources"
ClusterRolewhole clusterThe same, but not tied to a namespace. Also used for cluster-wide resources (nodes, namespaces)
RoleBindingone namespaceAttaches a Role or ClusterRole to a user, group or ServiceAccount, inside that namespace
ClusterRoleBindingwhole clusterAttaches a ClusterRole to a subject in every namespace
ServiceAccountone namespaceAn identity for a program running in a pod (people use users and groups)

A permission is a verb on a resource:

  • Verbs: get, list, watch (read), create, update, patch, delete, deletecollection (write).
  • Resources: pods, services, deployments, secrets, configmaps, and so on. Sub-resources are written with a slash: pods/log (read logs), pods/exec (open a shell), pods/portforward.
  • apiGroups: "" (empty) for the core group (pods, services, secrets, configmaps), apps for deployments, and so on. kubectl api-resources lists each resource with its group.

Subjects: who the binding applies to. Three kinds: User (a name), Group (a name that many users share) and ServiceAccount.

#The one idea that makes namespace permissions work

A RoleBinding can point at a ClusterRole. The ClusterRole defines what (a reusable job description), and the RoleBinding limits where (one namespace). So you write "developer" once and hand it out per namespace:

#Built-in ClusterRoles worth knowing

You rarely need to write a role from scratch. Kubernetes ships these:

ClusterRoleLets the subject
viewRead most objects in the namespace. Cannot read Secrets
editRead and change most objects, including Secrets, and run exec. Cannot change roles or bindings
adminEverything in the namespace, including roles and bindings there, but not the namespace object itself or its quota
cluster-adminEverything, everywhere. Bound at cluster level it is root

Lists them (without the many system: internal roles).

4.6 Bind the whole group, not the person. Anyone whose certificate says O=web-developers gets the same access, so you manage permissions per group and only the membership changes per person. Use the built-in edit role, scoped to web:

There is no way to revoke a client certificate. Kubernetes has no certificate revocation list. A leaked certificate stays valid until it expires. So issue short-lived certificates, and for real teams use SSO (OIDC), where access ends when the person's account does. To cut someone off immediately, remove the RoleBinding that grants their group.

#5. What a complete ACL for a cluster consists of

Permissions are not only RBAC. A complete setup has layers, each stopping a different kind of mistake or attack:

LayerQuestion it answersTool
1. AuthenticationWho is this?Client certificates (lab), OIDC / SSO (real), cloud IAM (GKE)
2. AuthorizationWhat may they do, and where?Roles, ClusterRoles, bindings
3. Workload identityWhat may a program do?One ServiceAccount per app, least permissions
4. AdmissionIs this object acceptable?Pod Security labels, quotas, policy engines
5. NetworkWhich pods may talk to which?NetworkPolicy
6. ResourcesHow much may a namespace use?ResourceQuota, LimitRange
7. SecretsWho can read credentials?RBAC on Secrets, encryption at rest
8. AuditWho did what, and who has access now?Audit logs, regular reviews

#5.1 Plan before you write YAML: personas and a matrix

Write down who needs what. Example for the namespaces web, cache and db:

WhowebcachedbCluster-wide
platform-adminsadminadminadmincluster-admin (very few people)
web-developerseditviewnonenone
db-adminsnonenoneadminnone
auditorsviewviewviewview
ci-deployer (a program)update Deploymentsnonenonenone

Rules to design by:

  • Bind groups, never individuals. Adding a person means adding them to a group, not editing RBAC.
  • Least privilege. Start from no access and add what is needed.
  • Prefer the built-in view, edit and admin bound per namespace with a RoleBinding. Write custom Roles only for gaps, such as the CI deployer.
  • Keep cluster-admin for a handful of people, and for nothing automated.
  • Separate duties: whoever can edit workloads in db is not automatically whoever can read its Secrets.

#5.2 Layers 1–2: bind the matrix

As YAML, so it can be reviewed and kept in git:

Each block is "who (subjects) gets which role (roleRef) where (namespace)". The last one is a ClusterRoleBinding, so auditors can read every namespace.

roleRef cannot be edited after creation. To change which role a binding points to, delete and re-create it.

#5.3 Layer 3: one ServiceAccount per app, with only what it needs

Pods run as the namespace's default ServiceAccount unless told otherwise, so give each app its own and give it nothing it does not use. A CI deployer that may only update Deployments in web:

#5.4 Layer 4: admission — Pod Security

RBAC says who may create a pod; Pod Security says what a pod may be (privileged, host networking, running as root). It is switched on per namespace with a label:

baseline blocks the clearly dangerous settings; restricted is stricter. Use pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=restricted first to see what would break without blocking anything.

#5.5 Layer 5: network — NetworkPolicy

By default every pod can reach every other pod in every namespace. A NetworkPolicy closes that. A common start is "deny all incoming traffic to db, then allow only what is needed":

podSelector: {} means every pod in the namespace. A NetworkPolicy does nothing unless the cluster's network plugin enforces it, and that depends on your setup and version. Check that kind's default plugin, or k3s's built-in controller, enforces policies before relying on it, or install a plugin that does (Calico, Cilium).

#5.7 Layer 7: secrets

  • view already excludes Secrets; edit and admin include them. Give those roles only where needed.
  • list on Secrets reveals their contents just like get does. Do not grant either casually.
  • Encrypt Secrets at rest on real clusters (a setting on the API server; managed clusters like GKE offer it).

#5.8 Layer 8: audit and review

Who can do something, and what can this identity do:

The last one lists every grant: look for cluster-admin bindings and for subjects you do not recognise.

On a real cluster, also turn on API audit logging (who did what, when) and review RBAC on a schedule: when people join, change teams or leave.

#6. Dangerous permissions: check these before you grant

Some permissions are much more powerful than they look:

PermissionWhy it is dangerous
* in verbs or resourcesEverything, including things added later
create on podsA pod can mount Secrets and ServiceAccount tokens in its namespace, so it can reach what the namespace holds
get / list on secretsReads every password and token in the namespace
pods/execA shell inside a running pod, with all its access
create on rolebindings or rolesCan grant themselves more power (Kubernetes blocks giving more than you hold, unless you also have escalate or bind)
escalate, bind, impersonateDirect ways to raise or borrow privileges
nodes/proxy, nodesReaches across the whole node
cluster-adminRoot

#7. On a managed cluster (GKE)

The same RBAC objects apply. Two additions:

  • Authentication and the first layer of permissions come from Google Cloud IAM. A person needs an IAM role (for example one that lets them reach the cluster) before Kubernetes RBAC is even asked.
  • Groups come from Google Groups (with Google Groups for RBAC enabled): bind the group's email in a RoleBinding, and managing membership happens in Google, not in Kubernetes.

So on GKE: IAM decides who may connect, RBAC decides what they may do in each namespace. Your lab cluster has no IAM, so certificates or tokens stand in for it.
